title: The debate judged by a garland
hookLine: a young monk walks to a great ritualist's door to argue, and the judge is the ritualist's wife
carry: truth is one; the wise call it by many names
tomorrow: a king finally sits down to eat after a long fast. then, a knock.

lines: A MONK LOOKING FOR ONE HOUSE.
cards: A young monk walks into a strange town, looking for one house. He asks the women at the well which one belongs to Mandana Mishra, the great master of the Vedic rites.
The story goes that they told him: look for the house where even the parrots at the door are arguing about the Vedas. The monk is Shankara. He hasn't come to visit.
He's come to debate. Today's summit sit climbs back to the schools of thought, the darshanas, through the most well-known argument the tradition tells.

teach.b: Here's how the Shankara Digvijaya, a much later life of Shankara, tells it. Mandana held the view of Mimamsa: the Vedas are above all a call to act, and the rites done rightly are the point.
Shankara held Vedanta: the rites prepare you, but freedom comes from knowing Brahman, the one reality. Who could judge them?

Mandana's wife, Ubhaya Bharati, a well-known scholar herself. She hung a fresh garland around each man's neck and said: whoever's garland wilts first has lost. The debate, the tradition says, ran for days.
At last Mandana's flowers began to fade. And the story doesn't end with a sneer.

Mandana became Shankara's student, and many remember him as Sureshvara, one of Shankara's great disciples. Then, the story says, Ubhaya Bharati challenged Shankara herself. That's the teaching under the story.
Hinduism never settled on one school of thought.

It kept its darshanas, a word that means seeing: Nyaya on how you know, Vaisheshika on what there is, Samkhya and Yoga on the witness and the stilled mind, Mimamsa on the rites, Vedanta on what is real.
Their teachers argued for centuries, and many teachers treat honest debate, shastrartha, as a way of serving the truth.

teach.h: TRUTH IS ONE; THE WISE CALL IT BY MANY NAMES.
teach.b: The Rig Veda put it early: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. So one family can hold a father who lives by the rites and a grandmother who lives by knowing, under one roof, and both are inside the tradition.
The path doesn't crown a winner. It asks you to argue the way Ubhaya Bharati judged: fairly, and with flowers on.

how: The darshanas are still studied through their root texts and commentaries in traditional schools and universities, and formal debate, shastrartha, is still held at some gatherings of scholars.

o: a well-known debate between two schools of thought, judged by a garland
a contest to decide which god is the strongest
a temple visit to see the deity at dawn

games.q: the garland debate — tap the pairs.
p: the rites done rightly are the point
judged the debate with two garlands
a way of seeing; a school of thought

s: the debate ended with Mandana mocked and sent away
in the story he became Shankara's student; many remember him as Sureshvara.
the judge of the debate was Mandana's own wife, a scholar
Ubhaya Bharati judged by two garlands: whoever's wilted first had lost.
Hinduism settled on one correct school of thought
it kept many darshanas, each a way of seeing, argued for centuries with no single winner.

games.q: you're Ubhaya Bharati. your own husband is debating a young monk, and you're the judge. how do you judge?
o: side with your husband, of course.
hang a fresh garland on each and watch whose wilts first.
stop the debate before anyone loses face.
games.why: she judged by the garlands, fairly, even with her husband on the line. in the tradition, honest argument is a way of serving the truth.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose view of God or religion differs from yours, at home or at work.

Picture a fresh garland around their neck and around yours, and say their view to yourself in its strongest, fairest form before you say your own. If you pray, ask to see the truth more clearly, whoever's flowers fade first.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the darshanas, Hinduism's schools of thought, argued hard and never ranked. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: darśana, seeing, a view; the word for a school of thought and for seeing the deity.

carryVoice: Your line: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Even a debate can be held with flowers on. Back tomorrow, same hill.
